one_sentence_story: Michael Posner proved in 1980 that even when your eyeballs stay frozen on a center cross, an invisible 'spotlight' of attention races out to a cued side in 100 milliseconds — speeding detection there while leaving uncued spots slower.
so_what_for_you: Remember that where your eyes point and where your mind aims can split completely: drivers staring straight ahead while mentally lost in a hands-free argument have pulled their spotlight off the road.

jargon_map.plain: shifting visual attention to a side location without moving your head or eyeballs
jargon_map.analogy: like listening intently to the table behind you at a café while looking straight at your menu

jargon_map.plain: a central arrow you voluntarily follow versus a sudden peripheral flash that grabs attention automatically
jargon_map.analogy: like choosing to scan a bookshelf vs jumping at a lightning flash

jargon_map.plain: the millisecond speedup when a target lands inside your spotlight plus the slowdown when you must disengage and re-aim
jargon_map.analogy: like guessing the right tennis corner early vs getting wrong-footed

jargon_map.plain: automatic suppression of an already-inspected flash spot after ~300 ms so you scan new places
jargon_map.analogy: like checking off a searched drawer so you don't open it twice
